source_text: Oremus itaque, fratres dilectissimi, sicut magister Deus docuit. amica et familiaris oratio est Deum de suo rogare, ad aures eius ascendere Christi orationem. agnoscat\'pater filii sui uerba, cum precem facimus: qui habitat intus in pectore ipse sit et in uoce, et cum ipsum habeamus aput patrem aduocatum pro peccatis nostris, quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus, aduocati nostri uerba promamus. nam cum dicat: quia quodcumque petierimus a patre in nomine eius dabit nobis, quanto efficacius impetramus quod petimus Christi nomine, si petamus ipsius oratione ?
orientation: Cyprian is addressing his fellow Christians, urging them to pray as Christ taught, because the Lord's Prayer is the Son's own prayer to the Father.
pass_a_gloss: Let us pray therefore, brothers most beloved, just as [the] master God taught. [a] friendly and familiar prayer it is God from his own to ask, to [the] ears of him to ascend [the] prayer of Christ. Let [the] father recognize [the] words of his son, when prayer we make: [he] who dwells within in [the] breast himself let him be also in [the] voice, and when him we have before [the] father [as] advocate for [the] sins our, when sinners for [the] offenses our we ask, [the] words of [the] advocate our let us bring forth. For since he says: because whatever we ask from [the] father in [the] name of him he will give to us, how much more effectively we obtain what we ask in [the] name of Christ, if we ask by [the] prayer of him?

choices.why: Cyprian's standard affectionate address to his fellow Christians; 'dilectissimi' is superlative, so 'most beloved' preserves the warmth and rank.

choices.english: to ask God with his own words
choices.why: The phrase 'de suo' means 'from his own [words]' or 'with what is his'; rendering it as 'with his own words' makes the sense clear in English while staying literal.
rejected: to ask God from his own
to ask God of his own

choices.term: ad aures eius ascendere Christi orationem
choices.english: to send up Christ's prayer to his ears
choices.why: The infinitive 'ascendere' is transitive here with 'orationem' as object; 'send up' keeps the upward motion and the direct object clear.
rejected: to ascend to his ears with Christ's prayer
to go up to his ears

choices.term: qui habitat intus in pectore ipse sit et in uoce
choices.english: let him who dwells inside in the breast be also in the voice
choices.why: The relative clause 'qui habitat intus in pectore' is the subject of 'sit'; keeping the relative clause as subject preserves the Latin structure and the idea that Christ dwelling within should also be in the spoken prayer.
rejected: he who dwells inside in the breast, let him also be in the voice

choices.english: let us bring forth the words of our advocate
choices.why: 'Promamus' is hortatory subjunctive; 'bring forth' captures the sense of producing or uttering the advocate's words in prayer.
rejected: let us offer the words of our advocate
let us speak the words of our advocate

choices.term: quanto efficacius impetramus quod petimus Christi nomine, si petamus ipsius oratione
choices.english: how much more effectively do we obtain what we ask in Christ's name, if we ask with his own prayer
choices.why: The comparative 'quanto efficacius' introduces a rhetorical question; keeping the question form and the comparative force preserves the argument's logic.
rejected: how much more effectively we obtain what we ask in Christ's name, if we ask with his own prayer

bible_refs.note: quodcumque petierimus a patre in nomine eius dabit nobis

pass_b_english: So let us pray, most beloved brothers, as God our teacher taught us. It is a friendly and familiar prayer to ask God with his own words, to send up Christ's prayer to his ears. Let the Father recognize his Son's words when we make our prayer. Let him who dwells inside in the breast be also in the voice, and since we have him as advocate with the Father for our sins, when we sinners plead for forgiveness of our offenses, let us bring forth the words of our advocate. For since he says that whatever we ask the Father in his name he will give us (John 16:23), how much more effectively do we obtain what we ask in Christ's name, if we ask with his own prayer?

last_rejected.quote: to send up Christ's prayer to his ears
last_rejected.source_quote: ad aures eius ascendere Christi orationem
last_rejected.why: Latin says Christ's prayer ascends to God's ears, not that we send it up.
last_rejected.fix: to let Christ's prayer ascend to his ears
last_rejected.ruling: 'ascendere' can mean 'to send up/offer'; English 'send up' conveys the prayer ascending to God's ears adequately.

last_rejected.quote: when we sinners ask for our offenses
last_rejected.source_quote: quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus
last_rejected.why: Latin says sinners ask FOR our offenses (forgiveness implied), not 'ask for our offenses' as objects sought.
last_rejected.fix: when we sinners ask for forgiveness of our offenses
last_rejected.ruling: 'petimus pro delictis' = ask on behalf of our offenses; 'ask for our offenses' is awkward but within acceptable range.

last_rejected.source_quote: quia quodcumque petierimus a patre in nomine eius dabit nobis
last_rejected.why: The quotation matches John 16:23 in Vulgate, but the clause 'in nomine eius' appears in John 16:23; however the fuller form with 'quodcumque petierimus a patre in nomine meo' is John 16:23. Check: this is actually John 16:23 or 1 John 5:14-15? The quote 'quodcumque petierimus... dabit nobis' with 'in nomine eius' is John 16:23. But 'dabit nobis' vs 'dabit vobis'—the source has 'nobis', which matches 1 John 3:22 or John 16:23? John 16:23 Vulgate has 'quodcumque petieritis Patrem in nomine meo dabit vobis'. The source's 'nobis' and 'eius' suggest this may be 1 John 3:22 or a mixed citation. The translator's John 16:23 may be incorrect.
last_rejected.ruling: Vulgate John 16:23 is the correct reference; Cyprian adapts 'vobis' to 'nobis' and 'meo' to 'eius' for his context.

problems.quote: when we sinners ask for our offenses
problems.source_quote: quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus
problems.why: "pro delictis petimus" means we plead on account of our offenses (for their pardon). "Ask for our offenses" suggests we request the offenses themselves.
problems.fix: when we sinners plead for our offenses to be forgiven, let us bring forth the words of our advocate.

edits.old: when we sinners ask for our offenses
edits.new: when we sinners plead for forgiveness of our offenses

fixed: Fixed mistranslation: Latin 'quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus' pleads on account of offenses for pardon, not requests the offenses themselves.

last_rejected.quote: when we sinners plead for forgiveness of our offenses
last_rejected.source_quote: quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus
last_rejected.why: Source says we sinners petition on behalf of our offenses (as advocate pleads); 'plead for forgiveness' adds forgiveness; 'forgiveness' not stated, though plausible.
last_rejected.fix: when we sinners petition for our offenses, let us bring forth the words of our advocate.
last_rejected.ruling: “petimus pro delictis nostris” means we petition concerning our offenses; “forgiveness” names the natural object, not a new claim.
